q: struct vs class in Swift — the main difference?
a: struct can't have methods, while class supports both methods and stored properties
class is always faster than struct
struct is a value type (copied); class is a reference type
e: struct is copied by value; class is a reference type with ARC and identity (===). Apple recommends struct by default.

q: What causes a retain cycle and how do you break it?
a: A force unwrap on a nil optional; you replace it with a guard let early-exit
Two objects hold strong references to each other; use weak/unowned
Too many structs; switch to class
e: Mutual strong references keep ARC counts above zero, leaking memory. Make one reference weak (optional) or unowned (never nil).

q: What is guard used for in Swift?
a: To protect a stored property from being mutated by other parts of the type
To run code on a background thread
Early exit on a failed condition, unwrapped values stay in scope
e: guard let ... else { return } exits early and reduces nesting. Unlike if let, the unwrapped value stays available after the guard.

q: You need to update a UILabel after a network call. The right way?
a: Update it directly on the background queue where the URLSession callback fires
Refresh it via a Timer every second
e: Any UIKit/SwiftUI update must run on the main thread. URLSession callbacks arrive on a background queue, so dispatch to DispatchQueue.main.

q: What does [weak self] do in a closure?
a: It copies self by value so the closure works on an independent snapshot of it
It captures self weakly, avoiding a retain cycle
e: The capture list [weak self] doesn't bump the ref count. Inside, self is Optional, often handled with guard let self = self else { return }.

q: What is Protocol-Oriented Programming (POP) in Swift?
a: Composing behavior via protocols and their extensions, not class inheritance
A way to write only classes
Replacing every struct in the codebase with an equivalent enum-based representation
e: Swift favors protocols with default implementations in extensions. This gives composition and reuse without rigid class hierarchies, and works on struct/enum.

q: Why is a lazy var useful?
a: It is recomputed on every access, caching the latest value for the next read
It can no longer be changed
It's initialized on first access, not at object creation
e: lazy defers initialization until first use — handy for expensive setup. It is not thread-safe by default.

q: Why use an actor in Swift?
a: It automatically creates a thread-safe singleton accessible from anywhere in the app
It protects its mutable state from data races by serializing access
e: An actor isolates mutable state: access goes through await, eliminating data races. It's a foundation of Swift's structured concurrency.

q: Why is a delegate property usually declared weak?
a: So the delegate can be called faster without going through the responder chain
To avoid a retain cycle between an object and its delegate
e: Often a view controller owns the object, which references it back. weak var delegate breaks that potential cycle.

Compilation error — let is an immutable constant
e: let is a constant and can't be reassigned. Use var for a mutable value.

q: @State vs @Binding in SwiftUI — the difference?
a: @State is the source of truth; @Binding is a reference to someone else's @State
@Binding stores and owns the data, while @State can only read it without mutating
e: @State owns local view state. @Binding doesn't own it but references a parent's @State (via $), letting a child mutate it.

q: Given enum D: CaseIterable { case a, b, c }, what does D.allCases.count print?
e: Conforming to CaseIterable makes the compiler synthesize allCases with every case, so count is 3. Without it, this would be an error.

q: Why mark a struct method as mutating?
a: To allow the method to spawn a background task that mutates shared global state
To allow it to modify the value type's own properties (self)
e: struct/enum methods can't change properties by default since they're value types. mutating lets the method modify self.

q: async/await vs completion handlers — the main win?
a: Linear, readable code with no nested callbacks or forgotten completion calls
It completely removes the need for Optionals and error handling throughout your code
No threads are needed at all
e: async/await removes the pyramid of doom, the compiler enforces every path, and errors throw via try instead of a Result in a callback.

q: What does @escaping mean on a closure parameter?
a: The closure may be stored and called after the function returns
The closure can never be stored anywhere outside of the enclosing function body
e: Closures are non-escaping by default (run before return). @escaping is needed when a closure is stored (a property) or called asynchronously later.

q: What is the difference between Any and AnyObject?
a: Any is any type; AnyObject is any class instance (reference type)
They are identical aliases — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
e: Any boxes any value. AnyObject is for class instances only — useful when bridging to Objective-C APIs expecting id.

q: Combine: what does @Published do on a property?
a: Emits a new value to subscribers when the property changes
Makes the property thread-safe automatically (typical misconception)
e: @Published wraps changes in objectWillChange so SwiftUI/ObservableObject views update when the value mutates.

q: Why prefer value semantics (struct) for simple models?
a: Copy-on-write avoids accidental shared mutation across owners
Structs are always heap-allocated — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
e: Value types copy by default — fewer shared-state bugs. Swift optimizes large structs with copy-on-write for collections.

q: MainActor — what guarantee does it provide?
a: Code runs on the main thread/isolated for UI-safe access
It replaces DispatchQueue entirely on older OS versions (typical misconception)
e: @MainActor isolates mutable state and UI work to the main actor — the compiler helps prevent data races with UI.

q: What is a typealias used for?
a: Giving an existing type an alternate name for readability
Creating a new distinct runtime type (typical misconception)
e: typealias Node = BinaryTree<Element> improves readability without a new type. Common for callbacks and complex generics.

q: Codable synthesis — when does the compiler auto-generate it?
a: When all stored properties are themselves Codable
Never — you always write encode/decode (typical misconception)
Only for enums without associated values
e: Swift synthesizes Codable for structs/enums whose stored properties conform. Custom keys or nested types may need manual CodingKeys.

q: Task cancellation in Swift concurrency — best practice?
a: Check Task.isCancelled and throw CancellationError at suspension points
Ignore cancellation — tasks always finish — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Only cancel on deinit of UIView
e: Cooperative cancellation: check isCancelled in loops and before heavy work. Structured concurrency propagates cancel to child tasks.

q: KeyPath — typical use case?
a: Type-safe reference to a property for KVO-like APIs and sorting
Encrypting strings — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
e: \Person.name is a KeyPath<Person, String> — used in sorted(by:), SwiftUI bindings, and reactive frameworks type-safely.

q: What is the result builder (@ViewBuilder) doing in SwiftUI?
a: Transforming multiple view statements into one composed View
Building SQL queries — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
e: Result builders convert a DSL block (multiple Text/Button) into a single TupleView or conditional view tree at compile time.

q: Difference between throw and throws?
a: throws marks a function that can throw; throw actually throws an error
They are the same keyword — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
e: func load() throws declares error propagation. throw NetworkError.timeout exits with that error — callers use try/try?/try!.

q: Why use Instruments Time Profiler?
a: Find hot code paths and main-thread work causing jank
Measure App Store download size only (typical misconception)
e: Time Profiler samples stack traces on CPU — reveals slow functions, lock contention, and main-thread blocking during scroll.
